summary:
Paraná is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework carried by the parent record; the findings below are those specific to the state and its municipalities.

Access to sex-separated facilities has been contested in Paraná's own legislature and in municipal councils. In 2021 state representative Mara Lima introduced a bill prohibiting unisex bathrooms statewide and requiring separate male and female facilities. On 16 November 2021 the Curitiba City Council approved a municipal bill of the same kind, introduced by councilman Ezequias Barros. The inventory does not record whether either measure was enacted.

On 4 October 2023 the Curitiba City Council approved, by symbolic vote, a motion of protest against Resolution 2/2023 of the federal Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, which had provided on 19 September 2023 that educational institutions must guarantee use of bathrooms, changing rooms and other gender-segregated spaces according to each student's gender identity and expression. The Ministry itself clarified that the resolution carries no binding effect and that no school is obliged to adopt it; the Curitiba motion was to be converted into an official letter to the federal government.

Gender-marker practice in Paraná's civil registries has moved in both directions. In 2023 the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná published a provision guaranteeing inclusion of a non-binary gender marker in the Civil Registry, then revoked it in November 2023, limiting administrative replacement of first name and sex to male and female only. In 2025 the same court authorized a third gender option on documents.

A municipal sports ban has been challenged and suspended. On 26 April 2024 Londrina enacted a law prohibiting transgender people from competing in sports according to their gender identity, with a R$10,000 fine for non-compliance. On 26 February 2026 the Londrina City Council approved a motion to bar transgender athlete Tiffanny Abreu from the Brazilian Women's Volleyball Cup; the Brazilian Volleyball Confederation filed suit in the Supreme Federal Court and Justice Cármen Lúcia issued a preliminary injunction the same day allowing her to compete. In March 2026 LGBTQ rights organisations filed suit against the Londrina law in the Supreme Federal Court, and on 7 August 2026 rapporteur Justice Cristiano Zanin voted to strike it down.

Paraná's own authorities moved ahead of the national position on relationship recognition. On 26 March 2013 the General Inspector of Justice of Paraná ruled that same-sex civil marriage must be granted in all cartórios statewide under the same procedure and documentation as different-sex marriage, and that a stable union could be converted into marriage without judicial authorization.
tangentialFactors:
The state-level and municipal hostility recorded in Paraná is directed at facilities and at sport rather than at the underlying legal status of trans people, which is set nationally. The Curitiba protest motion of 4 October 2023 was explicitly symbolic and targeted a federal resolution the issuing ministry had already said was non-binding.

Paraná's registry practice diverges from the national direction on gender markers: the state's Court of Justice published a non-binary marker provision in 2023, withdrew it later that year, then authorized a third gender option in 2025. The sequence leaves the operative rule dependent on the court's current internal instruction rather than on a published statute.

Historical items in the source inventory with no trans-specific bearing are not carried here, including the 1830 Imperial Penal Code's removal of sodomy references and the 13 June 2019 Supreme Federal Court rulings on racism-equivalent discrimination, which belong to the national record.
localsOnly:
Residents of Paraná have obtained relationship and family recognition through state courts before the national framework settled the position. On 14 May 2009 the 2nd Court of Childhood, Youth and Adoption granted the first adoption by a gay couple in Paraná to a Curitiba couple, finding a stable and affectionate union able to raise a child in a healthy environment. On 27 October 2010 a Cascavel judge, Sergio Luiz Kreuz, authorized the irreversible adoption of an eight-year-old child with cerebral palsy by a gay couple together twelve years, under Superior Court of Justice precedent. On 16 September 2011 Maringá justice authorized adoption of two children by a lesbian couple. In 2004 Curitiba recorded the first recognition of a same-sex union in Brazil, granting common-law marriage status to an English-Brazilian couple cohabiting fourteen years.

For residents, the practical question is which gender marker a Paraná registry will record. The Court of Justice of the State of Paraná's November 2023 revocation limited administrative replacement of first name and sex to male and female, while its 2025 authorization of a third gender option points the other way; the inventory does not resolve how the two interact at a given cartório.

The Londrina sports ban of 26 April 2024 carries a R$10,000 fine and applies to local competition, though a Supreme Federal Court preliminary injunction of 26 February 2026 and a rapporteur vote of 7 August 2026 both run against it.

Unresolved: whether the 2021 Paraná state bill and the 16 November 2021 Curitiba municipal bill prohibiting unisex bathrooms were enacted. The inventory records their introduction and approval in council only.

Unresolved: the final outcome of the Supreme Federal Court challenge to the Londrina law of 26 April 2024. The inventory records a rapporteur vote by Justice Cristiano Zanin on 7 August 2026 to strike the law down, not a final judgment of the full court.

Unresolved: how the Court of Justice of the State of Paraná's 2025 authorization of a third gender option interacts with its November 2023 revocation of the non-binary marker provision. No source in the inventory states which instruction governs current registry practice.

Not sourced: the inventory contains no Paraná-specific data on violence against trans people, on access to gender-affirming care in the state's public facilities, or on the treatment of trans people in the state's custody and prison system. National assessments on those points are carried by the parent record.
